phases.title: Wrist Armour & Hollow Line
phases.biomechanicalUnlock: Loaded wrist extension tolerance and a stacked hollow line. The desk bottleneck: keyboards keep wrists near neutral and never load them at 90 degrees of extension, while a stiff upper back and short lats stop the arms reaching fully overhead, so the lower back arches to make up the difference.

coreFocus.mechanicalSkill: Bear body weight on fully extended wrists without pain, and hold a hollow body with ribs down and arms by the ears.
coreFocus.mentalModel: A handstand is a stack of joints over a tiny base of support: your hands. Every degree of missing shoulder flexion gets paid back as arch in the lower back, which moves the centre of mass away from the middle of the hand and makes balance harder. Fix the stack before you try to balance it.

theoryConcepts: Joint stacking: wrist, shoulder, hip, ankle
Shoulder flexion to 180 degrees and the lat/thoracic limit
Hollow body = posterior pelvic tilt + ribs down

formCues.cue: Spread the hand, grip the floor
formCues.why: Fingers wide, knuckles pressed down. Load spreads across the whole palm instead of piling onto the heel of the hand and the back of the wrist.
Posterior pelvic tilt plus rib depression flattens the lower back. The inverted line is built from this shape.

formCues.cue: Push the floor away, ears covered
formCues.why: Full shoulder elevation locks the joint and lengthens the line; it is the difference between hanging on the shoulders and standing on them.

phases.frequency: 5-6 days/week, about 15 minutes. Low nervous-system cost, so it can follow your morning lift or sit at lunch or evening. Wrist prep is never skipped.

milestones.title: Pain-free wrist rocks
criteria: 30 s fingers-forward rocks at full lean, no pain during or the next morning.

milestones.title: Hollow 45 s
criteria: Legs straight, lower back pressed flat (a hand can't slide under).

milestones.title: Elevated pike 30 s
criteria: Hips stacked over shoulders, ears covered.

milestones.title: Phase 1 Gate: Joint Prep
criteria: 3 x 45 s hollow body holds, legs and arms straight, lower back glued to the floor.
Wall overhead test: back to the wall, thumbs touch the wall overhead while the lower back and ribs stay flat.
60 s plank on extended wrists with zero wrist pain during or 24 h after.
Elevated pike hold 3 x 30 s with hips stacked over shoulders.

dailyPractice.label: Wrist & shoulder prep
dailyPractice.task: Wrist CARs x5 each way. Quadruped wrist rocks: fingers forward x15, fingers back (palms up) x10, fist rocks x10. Finger-pad pulses (heel of hand lifts) x10. Arm circles and 10 scapular shrugs in a pike position.

dailyPractice.label: Hollow & overhead line
dailyPractice.task: Hollow body hold (knees bent until legs straight is possible). Back-to-wall arm slides: lower back flat, slide arms overhead toward the wall.
dailyPractice.prescription: Hollow 3 x 20-30 s; wall slides 2 x 10

dailyPractice.label: Loaded line
dailyPractice.task: Plank on extended wrists, then elevated pike hold: feet on a box or bench, walk hands back until hips stack over shoulders, push tall.
dailyPractice.prescription: Plank 3 x 30 s; elevated pike 3 x 20 s

offKeyboardHabit.title: Desk wrist reset
offKeyboardHabit.task: Once an hour or after each meeting: palms flat on the desk, fingers pointing toward you, lean gently for 10 s; then prayer and reverse-prayer stretch 10 s each; then 5 slow wrist CARs. About 60 seconds.

dos: Full wrist prep done and both wrists feel warm and pain-free when you lean into fingers-forward rocks.
Overhead check: back to the wall, arms up beside the ears, lower back stays flat. If it does not, spend 2 extra minutes on lat and upper-back mobility first.
Firm, non-slip floor (no socks on wood), space cleared around you.
donts: Don't load wrists cold, especially straight after a long typing block or a heavy pressing session.
Don't fake the overhead position by arching the lower back (banana back, rib flare). It looks like range but it is a broken stack.
Don't let the fingers lift and the heel of the hand take all the weight. That concentrates load where impingement happens.

stopRule.amber: A dull ache on the back of the wrist that doesn't clear after warm-up. Today: CARs and rocks in partial range plus hollow work only, no full-extension loading.
stopRule.red: Sharp pinch at the back of the wrist in extension, pain on the thumb or pinky side, clicking that hurts, or any tingling or numbness in the fingers. Stop all loaded wrist work for 48-72 hours. If it comes back on return, see a physio before continuing.

phaseLearningsPrompts: How far into a fingers-forward wrist rock did you first feel tension, and exactly where (back of wrist, forearm, palm)? How has that point moved over four weeks?
In the overhead wall test, what gave way first when you tried to keep your back flat: lats, upper back, or ribs popping forward?

phases.title: Chest-to-Wall Line & Heel Pulls
phases.biomechanicalUnlock: Inverted body awareness and the first balance correction: finger-pad braking. Facing the wall forces a straight line (back-to-wall lets you hang in a banana), and heel pulls teach the hand to create torque on demand with the wall as a safety net.

coreFocus.mechanicalSkill: Hold a straight chest-to-wall handstand with hands 10-20 cm from the wall, then lift the heels off the wall using finger pressure alone.
coreFocus.mentalModel: Your hand is a short lever. When the centre of mass drifts toward the fingers (overbalance), pressing the finger pads into the floor creates a torque that pushes it back over the palm. When it drifts toward the heel of the hand (underbalance), you push through the heel and lean the shoulders. A heel pull is the overbalance correction performed on purpose.

theoryConcepts: Line: wrists, shoulders, hips, ankles stacked
Active legs and pointed toes reduce wobble
Bail-outs: walk down and cartwheel exit

formCues.cue: Cambered fingers, brake with the pads
formCues.why: Slightly bent knuckles let the finger pads press like brakes. Flat fingers have no braking range.
Head neutral, eyes between the thumbs. Throwing the head back opens the ribs and arches the back.
A rigid body is one lever. A loose body is a chain of levers, and each link needs its own correction.

phases.frequency: 5-6 days/week, 15-20 minutes. Quality holds, not fatigue.

milestones.title: Chest-to-wall 30 s
criteria: 3 holds, side-view video shows wrist-shoulder-hip-ankle within a hand's width of vertical.

milestones.title: Toe pulls
criteria: 5 each leg, toe off the wall for 2 s.

milestones.title: Bail on demand
criteria: Cartwheel exit on both sides without hesitation.

milestones.title: Phase 2 Gate: Line & Brakes
criteria: 3 sets of 20 s chest-to-wall holds with hands within 15 cm of the wall, each set finishing with 5 controlled finger-press heel pulls (heels off the wall at least 2 s each).
One continuous 60 s chest-to-wall hold with no rib flare on video.
Cartwheel bail out of a wall kick-up on both sides.

dailyPractice.label: Wrist & shoulder prep
dailyPractice.task: Wrist CARs x5 each way. Quadruped wrist rocks: fingers forward x15, fingers back (palms up) x10, fist rocks x10. Finger-pad pulses (heel of hand lifts) x10. Arm circles and 10 scapular shrugs in a pike position.

dailyPractice.label: Chest-to-wall holds
dailyPractice.task: Walk feet up the wall and hands in until they are 10-20 cm from it. End each hold when the line breaks, not when the arms fail.

dailyPractice.label: Toe and heel pulls
dailyPractice.task: From chest-to-wall, press finger pads to lift one foot, then both heels, 1-2 cm off the wall. Hold, then return softly.

dailyPractice.label: Bail rehearsal
dailyPractice.task: From a small kick-up on grass or a mat, turn one hand and cartwheel out to the side.

offKeyboardHabit.title: Finger-pad desk press
offKeyboardHabit.task: Palms flat on the desk, lean forward slightly, press the finger pads until the heel of the hand nearly unweights. Hold 5 s, 5 reps, twice a day. This is the exact braking action of a handstand.

dos: Wrist status checked: green to proceed, amber means holds of 15 s or less.
Two practice cartwheel bails done before the first wall hold.
Hands measured at 10-20 cm from the wall, so the body is near vertical rather than a sloped plank.
donts: Don't hold until the arms shake and the shoulders sink. Failed reps teach failed balance.
Don't flare the ribs to get the chest closer to the wall.
Don't hold your breath through long holds. Breathe shallowly into a braced belly.

stopRule.amber: Wrist ache building through the session or a pinch at the front of the shoulder. Cut holds to 15 s and stop heel pulls for today.
stopRule.red: Sharp shoulder or wrist pain, a headache or pressure behind the eyes when inverted, or dizziness that doesn't settle within seconds of coming down. End the session. Inversions are not advised with uncontrolled high blood pressure or glaucoma; check with a doctor if either applies.

phaseLearningsPrompts: During heel pulls, how much finger pressure did it take to move your heels: a light touch or a hard grip? Did it differ between hands?
On your side-view video, where does the line break first: hips piking, lower back arching, or shoulders closing?

phases.title: Tuck & Scissor Entries
phases.biomechanicalUnlock: Controlled entry. A kick-up is a pendulum: you need exactly enough angular momentum to reach the balance point. A tuck shortens the body's radius, lowers its moment of inertia and makes momentum easier to meter; the scissor kick then lengthens it again.

coreFocus.mechanicalSkill: From the floor, arrive at a stacked line with the minimum kick and hold 3-5 s freestanding before stepping down or bailing.
coreFocus.mentalModel: Over-kick and you carry too much angular momentum past the balance point. Under-kick and you never get there. Shift the shoulders over the hands first, so the legs only have to travel the last short arc. Tucking the knees makes the swing slower and easier to stop; extend the legs only once you are stacked.

theoryConcepts: Angular momentum and the pendulum kick
Moment of inertia: tuck vs straight
Balance point = centre of mass over the middle of the hand
Hand spacing for wall kick-ups (~30 cm)

formCues.cue: Shoulders over hands before the feet leave
formCues.why: Weight shifts first, kick second. Kicking into sloped shoulders guarantees an under-balance.

formCues.cue: Kick to the ceiling, not to the wall
formCues.why: Aim the legs at the stacked point. The wall is a backstop, not a target.
Knees to chest makes the swing slow and controllable; extend only once the hips are over the hands.

phases.frequency: 5-6 days/week, about 20 minutes. Cap attempts per session.

milestones.title: Frog hop hold
criteria: 3 s tucked hold, 5 in a row.

milestones.title: Light-touch wall arrivals
criteria: 8 of 10 kick-ups arrive without a thud.

milestones.title: First free catch
criteria: 3 s freestanding from a kick-up.

milestones.title: Phase 3 Gate: Entries
criteria: From the floor, a tuck or scissor kick-up held freestanding for 5 s, in 5 of 10 attempts.
8 of 10 wall kick-ups arrive with a light heel touch.
45 s chest-to-wall hold with a straight line maintained.

dailyPractice.label: Wrist & shoulder prep
dailyPractice.task: Wrist CARs x5 each way. Quadruped wrist rocks: fingers forward x15, fingers back (palms up) x10, fist rocks x10. Finger-pad pulses (heel of hand lifts) x10. Arm circles and 10 scapular shrugs in a pike position.

dailyPractice.label: Tuck jumps (frog hops)
dailyPractice.task: Hands on the floor, hop the hips up over the shoulders in a tight tuck and hold, then lower softly.

dailyPractice.label: Wall kick-ups
dailyPractice.task: Hands about 30 cm from the wall. Lunge kick and aim to arrive with the lightest possible touch of the heels.

dailyPractice.label: Free kick-ups
dailyPractice.task: Open space on grass or a mat. Kick, catch the balance for 1-5 s, then step down or cartwheel out.

dailyPractice.label: Line maintenance
dailyPractice.task: Chest-to-wall hold with heel pulls.

offKeyboardHabit.title: Split-stance hip opener
offKeyboardHabit.task: Desk hours shorten the hip flexors, which blunts the scissor kick. Each afternoon: half-kneeling hip flexor stretch with a glute squeeze, 2 x 30 s per side, and 10 leg swings per leg on your walk.

dos: 2 m of clear space around you, on grass or a mat.
Two rehearsed bails before the first free attempt.
Attempt cap decided before you start (for example, 15).
donts: Don't kick hard to get up. Big kicks build an over-balance habit and slam you into the wall.
Don't land on bent arms or your head. Turn a hand and cartwheel out.
Don't keep going once quality drops. Three bad kicks in a row ends the session.

stopRule.amber: Accumulating wrist ache from repeated landings, or shoulder fatigue making arrivals sloppy. Switch to wall holds only for the rest of the session.
stopRule.red: A fall onto the head or neck, sharp wrist pain on landing, or dizziness. Stop for the day, and get any neck pain checked.

phaseLearningsPrompts: On your best kick-ups, what did your shoulders do before your legs left the floor? Describe the moment of arrival.
Which correction do you use more: finger press (over-balance) or heel-of-hand push (under-balance)? What does that say about your kick?

phases.title: Freestanding Balance
phases.biomechanicalUnlock: Fine-motor balance. Corrections move from big hip and shoulder movements down to small, continuous adjustments at the wrists and fingers. This phase trains the proprioceptive control loop.

coreFocus.mechanicalSkill: Hold a straight freestanding handstand for 30 s, correcting through the fingers and palm instead of arching or walking.
coreFocus.mentalModel: Balance is a feedback loop: sense drift, apply hand torque, re-stack. The hand can only correct a small drift of the centre of mass, a few centimetres, because its torque range is limited by its length. Bigger errors need a shoulder-angle change or a step. So the skill is catching errors while they are tiny. Live slightly on the finger pads so you always have a correction ready.

theoryConcepts: Hand torque range and its limits
Straight line vs banana vs straddle
Practice density: many short good holds over few long bad ones

formCues.why: Sit slightly toward the finger pads so a correction is always loaded and ready.
Shoulder elevation keeps the base stable; a sinking shoulder is a moving base.
A 1 cm drift is a finger correction. A 5 cm drift is a step.

phases.frequency: 5-6 days/week, about 20 minutes. Stop the session when holds start getting shorter.

milestones.title: 10 s club
criteria: 5 holds of 10 s in one session.

milestones.title: 20 s
criteria: Best hold at least 20 s.

milestones.title: Back-to-back
criteria: 3 consecutive kick-ups each held 10 s.

milestones.title: Phase 4 Gate: Freestanding
criteria: Freestanding handstand of 30 s with a straight line (no visible arch on video), in 3 of 5 attempts in one session.
Average hold of at least 15 s across 10 attempts.
Every hold ends in a controlled step-down, not a fall.

dailyPractice.label: Wrist & shoulder prep
dailyPractice.task: Wrist CARs x5 each way. Quadruped wrist rocks: fingers forward x15, fingers back (palms up) x10, fist rocks x10. Finger-pad pulses (heel of hand lifts) x10. Arm circles and 10 scapular shrugs in a pike position.

dailyPractice.label: Free hold attempts
dailyPractice.task: Kick up to a freestanding hold, up to 30 s each. Log the best and the average.

dailyPractice.label: Wall-free holds
dailyPractice.task: Chest-to-wall, pull both heels off and balance free with the wall as a net.

dailyPractice.label: Shape changes
dailyPractice.task: On the wall: straight to tuck to straddle and back.

offKeyboardHabit.title: Eyes-closed single-leg balance
offKeyboardHabit.task: While brushing your teeth or waiting for the kettle: single-leg balance with eyes closed, 30 s per leg. It trains the same ankle-and-foot sensing loop the hands use upside down.

dos: Wrist status green.
Bail rehearsed twice.
You are fresh: not straight after a max-effort pressing session.
donts: Don't chase the timer with a banana back. A long ugly hold teaches the wrong line.
Don't walk on your hands to save every attempt. It hides the balance problem you are here to fix.
Don't train to fatigue. The last tired attempts are the ones your nervous system remembers.

stopRule.amber: Dull ache on the back of the wrist or tight forearms. Halve today's attempts and add 2 minutes of forearm stretching.
stopRule.red: Sharp pinch at the back of the wrist in extension, pain on the thumb or pinky side, clicking that hurts, or any tingling or numbness in the fingers. Stop all loaded wrist work for 48-72 hours. If it comes back on return, see a physio before continuing. Elbow pain also counts.

phaseLearningsPrompts: Where on your hand is your weight during your best holds: finger pads, mid-palm, or heel? Map it.
What time of day, and after what (typing, gym, rest day), do you get your longest holds? Log best vs average.

phases.title: Mastery: Consistency & Press Foundations
phases.biomechanicalUnlock: Automaticity. Balance becomes unconscious, which frees attention for shape changes and builds the compression and shoulder-lean strength behind a press to handstand.

coreFocus.mechanicalSkill: Kick up on demand and hold 60 s; change shapes mid-hold; start press foundations.
coreFocus.mentalModel: Mastery is consistency, not your best-ever hold. Each shape change moves the centre of mass (a straddle brings it toward the hands, a tuck lowers it), so the shoulders must lean to keep it over the base. In a press, the shoulders lean forward past the hands while the legs compress close to the torso, keeping the combined centre of mass over the hands the whole way up.

theoryConcepts: Shape changes move the centre of mass

formCues.cue: Lean shoulders to match the legs
formCues.why: When the legs come down toward a straddle or press, the shoulders go forward by the same amount of mass-weighted distance.
Pull the legs in tight first; a short lever is easier to lift over the hands.
Train cold-start reliability. That is what a handstand on demand means.

phases.frequency: 5-6 days/week, 20-25 minutes. Press work only 2x/week, and never on dragon flag days (both are heavy compression).

milestones.title: 45 s hold
criteria: Straight line, freestanding.

milestones.title: Shape cycle
criteria: Straight, straddle, tuck, straight in one hold.

milestones.title: Press negatives
criteria: 3 straddle press negatives with 3 s descent.

milestones.title: Phase 5 Gate: Mastery
criteria: 60 s freestanding straight handstand.
First-attempt reliability: on 8 of 10 separate cold starts across a week, the first kick-up holds at least 10 s.
One hold that moves straight, straddle, tuck, straight without falling.

dailyPractice.label: Wrist & shoulder prep
dailyPractice.task: Wrist CARs x5 each way. Quadruped wrist rocks: fingers forward x15, fingers back (palms up) x10, fist rocks x10. Finger-pad pulses (heel of hand lifts) x10. Arm circles and 10 scapular shrugs in a pike position.

dailyPractice.label: First-attempt test
dailyPractice.task: Five kick-ups; log whether the first one held 10 s.

dailyPractice.label: Long holds & shapes
dailyPractice.task: Freestanding holds with mid-hold shape changes: straight, straddle, tuck, straight.

dailyPractice.label: Press foundations (2x/week)
dailyPractice.task: Seated pike compression lifts; elevated straddle press negatives from a box, lowering slowly from handstand.
dailyPractice.prescription: Compression 3 x 10; negatives 3 x 3 with 3 s descent

offKeyboardHabit.title: Seated compression lifts
offKeyboardHabit.task: Sitting on the front edge of your chair, hands beside the hips, lift both feet and hold 5 s. 5 reps, twice a day. This builds hip-flexor compression without loading the wrists.

dos: Wrist status green.
No dragon flag session today if pressing.
Log the first attempt before anything else.
donts: Don't skip wrist prep because you're good now. Tendons adapt more slowly than skill.
Don't stack press work on dragon flag days.
Don't jump to one-arm or press-from-floor work before the 60 s gate.

stopRule.amber: Wrist or forearm ache. Drop press work for the week; keep holds short.
stopRule.red: Sharp pinch at the back of the wrist in extension, pain on the thumb or pinky side, clicking that hurts, or any tingling or numbness in the fingers. Stop all loaded wrist work for 48-72 hours. If it comes back on return, see a physio before continuing.

phaseLearningsPrompts: When you hit 60 s, what were you actually thinking about? Did balance feel automatic or effortful?
How many pain-free wrist days per week do you have now compared with Phase 1?

phases.title: Hollow Body & Pelvic Control
phases.biomechanicalUnlock: Anti-extension: locking the pelvis in posterior tilt while the legs pull on it. The desk bottleneck: hours of sitting shorten the hip flexors (psoas, rectus femoris), which tip the pelvis forward and drag the lower back into an arch as soon as the legs straighten.

coreFocus.mechanicalSkill: Hold a posterior pelvic tilt with ribs down while the legs are extended.
coreFocus.mentalModel: Your legs are a weight on the end of a lever pivoting at the hips. As they lower, the hip flexors pull on the lumbar spine and try to arch it. Abs and glutes must win that tug of war by locking the pelvis in posterior tilt. A dragon flag is the same fight with the pivot moved up to the shoulders, so the lever gets longer and the fight gets harder.

theoryConcepts: Hip flexor pull on the lumbar spine
Hollow body as the dragon flag shape on the floor

formCues.cue: Zip the belt line to the floor
formCues.why: Posterior pelvic tilt removes the lumbar arch before load arrives.
A forceful exhale pulls the ribs down and switches on the deep abdominals.

formCues.cue: Reach the heels long, not up
formCues.why: Length lowers the legs without letting them pull the pelvis forward.

phases.frequency: 3x/week, 10-12 minutes, after a gym session or on its own. Non-consecutive days.

milestones.title: Dead bug 10/side
criteria: 3 s exhale per rep, back never lifts.

milestones.title: Hollow 45 s
criteria: Legs straight.

milestones.title: Couch stretch 60 s
criteria: Each side, glute on, torso upright.

milestones.title: Phase 1 Gate: Pelvic Lock
criteria: 60 s hollow body hold, legs straight, arms overhead, lower back flat (hand-under test fails to slide).
3 x 12 reverse crunches with a 3 s lowering.
Couch stretch with knee down, glute squeezed and torso upright for 60 s per side.

dailyPractice.label: Dead bugs
dailyPractice.task: Lower back pressed down. Extend opposite arm and leg on a slow 3 s exhale.

dailyPractice.label: Hollow body hold
dailyPractice.task: Progress from bent knees to straight legs to arms overhead only when the back stays flat.

dailyPractice.label: Reverse crunch
dailyPractice.task: Curl the hips off the floor, lower over 3 s.

dailyPractice.label: Couch stretch
dailyPractice.task: Half-kneeling, rear shin up a wall or sofa, glute squeezed, torso upright.

offKeyboardHabit.title: Stand-up glute reset
offKeyboardHabit.task: Every time you stand from the desk: squeeze the glutes and tuck the pelvis for 5 s. Twice a day, a standing lunge hip-flexor stretch, 30 s per side.

dos: Low-back test: lying down, you can press your lower back flat with a posterior tilt.
Hip flexor stretch done today.
Breathing plan: exhale through every hard part of the rep.
donts: Don't let the lower back arch to make a hold last longer.
Don't pull on the neck or poke the chin.
Don't take every set to failure. Stop with 1-2 good reps left.

stopRule.amber: Low-back pump or fatigue, or a cramp at the front of the hip. Shorten the lever (bend the knees) and drop a set.
stopRule.red: A sharp pinch in the lower back, pain spreading into the buttock or leg, numbness or tingling, or neck pain that travels into the arm. Stop all core loading today. If it lasts more than 48 hours or keeps returning, see a physio.

phaseLearningsPrompts: When your legs straighten in the hollow, how low can they go before your back lifts? Estimate the angle off the floor.
Left vs right: does one hip flexor feel tighter in the couch stretch? Note which.

phases.title: Tuck Flag: Tripod & Eccentric Control
phases.biomechanicalUnlock: The upper-back tripod: shoulders and upper back become the pivot, the hands anchor by pulling on the bench, and the tuck shortens the lever to roughly half the full-flag torque.

coreFocus.mechanicalSkill: Hold a tuck dragon flag at 45 degrees and lower it slowly with hips open.
coreFocus.mentalModel: Torque at the shoulders = body weight x horizontal distance to your centre of mass. Tucking the knees pulls that centre of mass toward the shoulders and roughly halves the demand. Torque also changes with angle: near vertical it is close to zero, and it peaks at horizontal (it scales with the cosine of the angle from the bench). So the last 30 degrees before the bench is where form breaks.

formCues.why: Weight sits on the shoulder blades and upper back, never on the neck. The two hands plus upper back form the base.

formCues.cue: Pull the bench toward your head
formCues.why: Lats on. They stabilise the shoulder pivot and take load off the neck.

formCues.cue: Hips stay open in the tuck
formCues.why: Knees bend but the hip angle stays straight: shoulders to knees is one line. A hip bend turns it into a reverse crunch.

phases.frequency: 2x/week, never on consecutive days, about 15 minutes. Counts as a heavy core day.

milestones.title: Candlestick 30 s
criteria: Vertical, neck free.

milestones.title: Tuck hold 45 degrees
criteria: 15 s with hips open.

milestones.title: Slow tuck negatives
criteria: 4 reps at 5 s each.

milestones.title: Phase 2 Gate: Tuck Flag
criteria: 4 tuck dragon flag eccentrics with a 5 s descent, hips staying open (shoulder-to-knee line straight), stopped 10 cm above the bench.
3 x 15 s tuck holds at 45 degrees.
30 s candlestick hold.

dailyPractice.label: Warm-up
dailyPractice.task: Dead bugs and a 30 s hollow hold.

dailyPractice.label: Candlestick hold
dailyPractice.task: Setup: lie on a flat, stable bench, grip the bench edge (or a fixed post) behind your head, roll up to vertical with weight on the upper back and shoulder blades. Hold the body vertical.

dailyPractice.label: Tuck eccentrics
dailyPractice.task: From vertical, lower in a tuck over 5 s to just above the bench. Return to the top with help (roll up).

dailyPractice.label: Tuck hold at 45 degrees
dailyPractice.task: Hips open, shoulder-to-knee line straight.

offKeyboardHabit.title: Desk lat isometric
offKeyboardHabit.task: Hands under the desk edge, pull upward as if to lift it, squeeze the lats and keep the shoulders down. 5 x 10 s. This is the bench-pull you use in the tripod.

dos: Bench is stable and the anchor point cannot move.
Warm-up done: dead bugs and a hollow hold.
Neck check at the top: weight on the shoulder blades, neck free.
donts: Don't pike at the hips. Sagging hips shorten the lever and fake progress.
Don't drop through the bottom 30 degrees.
Don't swing or kick up into the top position.

stopRule.amber: Neck strain or tight upper traps. Stop the set, reset grip and shoulders, and halve the remaining volume.
stopRule.red: A sharp pinch in the lower back, pain spreading into the buttock or leg, numbness or tingling, or neck pain that travels into the arm. Stop all core loading today. If it lasts more than 48 hours or keeps returning, see a physio.

phaseLearningsPrompts: At what angle does the descent start to speed up against your will? Mark it.
Where do you feel the load: abs, lats or hip flexors? Does it change as you approach horizontal?

phases.title: Lengthening the Lever: Single-Leg & Straddle
phases.biomechanicalUnlock: Progressive lever lengthening between tuck and full flag: advanced tuck (knees at 90 degrees), then one leg extended, then straddle. Each step moves the centre of mass further from the shoulder pivot.

coreFocus.mechanicalSkill: Lower and hold single-leg and straddle flags with a straight torso line and no hip rotation.
coreFocus.mentalModel: Single-leg extension sits about halfway between tuck and full in torque. A straddle shortens the lever less than people think: angling the legs out only shortens their projection along the body by about 5-10%. Its real benefit is that it is easier to hold posterior tilt with the legs apart. So the order is tuck, advanced tuck, single-leg, straddle, full.

theoryConcepts: Straddle: small lever change, easier pelvic control
Progress by angle and by lever

formCues.why: Both hip bones face the ceiling; the extended leg must not twist the pelvis.
A soft knee shortens the lever without you noticing.
Re-set the upper-back pressure before every rep.

milestones.title: Advanced tuck eccentrics
criteria: 3 reps at 5 s.

milestones.title: Single-leg each side
criteria: 3 reps per side at 4 s.

milestones.title: Straddle 45 degrees
criteria: 5 s hold.

milestones.title: Phase 3 Gate: Long Lever
criteria: 3 single-leg dragon flag eccentrics per side, 5 s descent, no hip pike, no rotation.
3 x 8 s straddle dragon flag holds at 45 degrees.
3 advanced-tuck reps up and down (3 s lower, controlled raise).

dailyPractice.label: Warm-up
dailyPractice.task: Dead bugs, hollow hold, 2 easy tuck negatives.

dailyPractice.label: Advanced tuck eccentrics
dailyPractice.task: Setup: lie on a flat, stable bench, grip the bench edge (or a fixed post) behind your head, roll up to vertical with weight on the upper back and shoulder blades. Knees at 90 degrees, lower over 5 s.

dailyPractice.label: Single-leg eccentrics
dailyPractice.task: One leg extended, the other tucked; alternate legs per set.

dailyPractice.label: Straddle hold
dailyPractice.task: Legs wide, hold at 45 degrees.

offKeyboardHabit.title: Wall pelvic-tilt reps
offKeyboardHabit.task: During a coffee break: stand with your back to a wall, flatten the lower back into it with a posterior tilt, hold 3 s. 10 reps. It rehearses the exact pelvic position under no load.

dos: Warm-up and tuck negatives done.
Bench stable, grip anchored.
Decide the lever for today before starting, and don't upgrade it mid-session.
donts: Don't bend the 'straight' leg to finish a rep. Log it as an easier lever instead.
Don't let the hips rotate toward the extended leg.
Don't grind through form breakdown. One clean rep is worth more than three ugly ones.

stopRule.amber: One-sided low-back soreness the next day. Return to advanced tuck for a week.
stopRule.red: A sharp pinch in the lower back, pain spreading into the buttock or leg, numbness or tingling, or neck pain that travels into the arm. Stop all core loading today. If it lasts more than 48 hours or keeps returning, see a physio.

phaseLearningsPrompts: Which leg extended feels harder? Is there a rotation tendency to one side?
Rate each lever step 1-10 for effort. Where was the biggest jump?

phases.title: Full Dragon Flag Negatives
phases.biomechanicalUnlock: Full-lever eccentric strength. Muscles can resist about 20-40% more load while lengthening than they can lift, so the full flag is built from the top down before it is ever raised.

coreFocus.mechanicalSkill: Lower a straight-body dragon flag over 5 s to a hover just above the bench.
coreFocus.mentalModel: With legs straight, roughly a third of your body mass sits at the far end of the lever, and torque near horizontal is about double the tuck version. Treat the body as one plank hinged only at the shoulders. Any bend at the hips is the lever cheating you.

theoryConcepts: Recovery: eccentrics cause the most soreness

formCues.why: Shoulders are the only joint that moves.

formCues.cue: Slow the bottom, not the top
formCues.why: Spend most of the 5 s in the last 30 degrees where torque is highest.
Keeps ribs down as the lever gets heavier.

milestones.title: First full negative
criteria: Straight body, 3 s descent.

milestones.title: 5 s negatives
criteria: 3 reps at 5 s.

milestones.title: Hover
criteria: 3 s at horizontal.

milestones.title: Phase 4 Gate: Full Negative
criteria: 5 strict full dragon flag eccentrics with a 5 s descent and zero hip hinge, ending in a hover 10 cm above the bench.
3 x 5 s hover holds at the bottom.

dailyPractice.label: Warm-up
dailyPractice.task: Hollow hold, 2 straddle negatives.

dailyPractice.label: Full negatives
dailyPractice.task: Setup: lie on a flat, stable bench, grip the bench edge (or a fixed post) behind your head, roll up to vertical with weight on the upper back and shoulder blades. Lower straight over 5 s. Rest 2-3 min between sets.

dailyPractice.label: Hover holds
dailyPractice.task: Hold just above the bench.

dailyPractice.label: Top-range partials
dailyPractice.task: From vertical, lower 30 degrees, then raise back.

offKeyboardHabit.title: Hip extension reset
offKeyboardHabit.task: After work: 10 glute bridges with a 2 s squeeze, then the couch stretch 30 s per side. Long sitting undoes your pelvic control; this puts it back.

dos: At least 72 hours since the last flag session.
No low-back soreness from yesterday's lifting.
Warm-up negatives felt smooth.
donts: Don't hinge at the hips to save the bottom of the rep.
Don't kick or swing into the top before the negative.
Don't train flags more than twice a week in this phase.

stopRule.amber: Ab soreness is normal; low-back soreness the next day is not. If the back is sore, regress to straddle for a week.
stopRule.red: A sharp pinch in the lower back, pain spreading into the buttock or leg, numbness or tingling, or neck pain that travels into the arm. Stop all core loading today. If it lasts more than 48 hours or keeps returning, see a physio.

phaseLearningsPrompts: On video, is your 5 s evenly spread, or do you hang at the top and drop at the bottom?
How long until your core felt fully recovered after a negative session: 48 or 72 hours?

phases.title: Strict Concentric Dragon Flag
phases.biomechanicalUnlock: Concentric strength through the sticking point. The hardest moment is the first 20 degrees up from horizontal, where torque peaks and there is no momentum to help.

coreFocus.mechanicalSkill: Raise a straight-body dragon flag from a hover to vertical, then string reps together.
coreFocus.mentalModel: Lead with the lats by pulling the bench, and keep the posterior tilt locked. The moment the pelvis tips forward, the straight lever becomes a banana and the load shifts onto the lumbar spine. 'Dragon fly' is the same movement in gym slang; mastery here means strict reps with no hip bend.

formCues.why: Lats fire first and the body follows as one lever.
No forward tilt at the hardest point.
Paused reps build strength exactly where it fails.

phases.frequency: 2x/week; 3x/week only when the handstand press work and marathon peak are not in the same week. Cap: 15 quality reps per session.

milestones.title: First strict raise
criteria: Hover to vertical, no hip bend.

milestones.title: 3 singles
criteria: In one session.

milestones.title: 1 x 3
criteria: Three strict reps in a row.

milestones.title: Phase 5 Gate: Strict Dragon Flag
criteria: 3 strict dragon flags in a row: 5 s lower, 2 s hover, controlled raise, zero hip pike, no momentum.
Mastery marker: 2 sets of 5 strict reps with 3 s eccentrics.

dailyPractice.label: Warm-up
dailyPractice.task: Hollow hold, 2 negatives.

dailyPractice.label: Concentric singles
dailyPractice.task: From a hover, raise to vertical. Full rest between attempts.

dailyPractice.label: Negative-to-raise reps
dailyPractice.task: Lower 5 s, raise 3 s.

dailyPractice.label: Paused reps
dailyPractice.task: Pause 2 s at 45 degrees on the way down.

offKeyboardHabit.title: Couch stretch + PPT
offKeyboardHabit.task: Keep the daily hip-flexor stretch going: it is what lets you hold posterior tilt at the sticking point.

dos: 72 hours since the last flag session (48 if running 3x/week flags).
No long run tomorrow if this is the third weekly session.
Warm-up negatives clean.
donts: Don't pike the hips to get through the sticking point.
Don't use momentum from a swing.
Don't add reps by losing tempo. Log strict reps only.

stopRule.amber: Lower-back fatigue before the core is tired. End the session; do negatives only next time.
stopRule.red: A sharp pinch in the lower back, pain spreading into the buttock or leg, numbness or tingling, or neck pain that travels into the arm. Stop all core loading today. If it lasts more than 48 hours or keeps returning, see a physio.

phaseLearningsPrompts: At which angle is your sticking point? Has it moved over the phase?
Compare your hollow body hold time now with Phase 1. What changed in how it feels?

program.title: Marathon Running Engine
program.archetype: Aerobic periodisation, stride mechanics & tissue resilience

phases.title: Cadence & Tissue Adaptation
phases.biomechanicalUnlock: Musculoskeletal tolerance and stride mechanics. Your gym-trained heart and lungs will adapt within weeks, but bone, tendon and calf capacity take months. The desk bottleneck: under-used calves and soleus, weak shins and tight hip flexors that limit hip extension, which pushes the foot out in front of the body.

coreFocus.mechanicalSkill: Run 30 minutes continuously at an easy effort with a short stride that lands under your hips.
coreFocus.mentalModel: Overstriding puts the foot down ahead of your centre of mass, which acts as a brake on every step and increases loading at the knee and shin. Raising cadence about 5-10% shortens the stride and moves the landing closer to under the body. 170+ steps per minute is a useful guide, not a law: find your natural cadence and nudge it up. Where the foot lands relative to the hips matters more than whether the heel or midfoot touches first.

theoryConcepts: Effort by RPE and the talk test

formCues.why: Foot touches down close to beneath the centre of mass with a soft knee.
Your natural cadence plus 5%, around 170 for most people. A metronome app helps.
Hips forward, not sitting back. Opens up the hip extension sitting takes away.

phases.frequency: 3 runs/week on non-consecutive days (e.g. Tue/Thu/Sat), 20-35 minutes. Calf and shin conditioning 3x/week, which can attach to your gym session.

milestones.title: 20 min continuous
criteria: Conversational pace.

milestones.title: Cadence logged
criteria: Natural cadence measured, target set at +5%.

milestones.title: Calf capacity
criteria: 20 single-leg calf raises per side.

milestones.title: Phase 1 Gate: Chassis
criteria: Three 30 min continuous runs in one week at a conversational pace, with no shin or calf pain the next morning.
Average cadence within 5% of your target over 20 minutes (watch or phone).
25 single-leg calf raises per side through full range, and 20 tibialis raises.

dailyPractice.label: Run-walk
dailyPractice.task: Week 1: 8 x (2 min jog, 1 min walk). Build to 30 min continuous by week 6. RPE 3-4/10, full sentences possible.

dailyPractice.label: Cadence drill
dailyPractice.task: 4 x 20 s at your natural cadence plus 5% to a metronome.

dailyPractice.label: Strides (from week 3)
dailyPractice.task: Relaxed fast running on flat ground, full walk-back recovery.

dailyPractice.label: Tissue conditioning
dailyPractice.task: Straight-knee calf raises and bent-knee (soleus) raises with 3 s lowering; tibialis raises against a wall; single-leg balance.
dailyPractice.prescription: Calf 3 x 15 each type; tib 3 x 20; balance 3 x 30 s

offKeyboardHabit.title: Tibialis raises on calls
offKeyboardHabit.task: Back against a wall, heels 30 cm out, lift the toes and forefoot up and down. 2 x 20 during a call. Calf raises while the kettle boils.

dos: Shin and calf check: run fingers along the inner shin (no pinpoint pain) and do 10 single-leg hops each side pain-free.
Shoes checked: under roughly 600-800 km of wear.
5 min warm-up: brisk walk and leg swings.
donts: Don't increase weekly running time or distance by more than 10%, and take a cutback week every 4th week.
Don't overstride to go faster. Speed comes from cadence and fitness, not a reaching foot.
Don't run every run moderately hard. Easy days are easy.

stopRule.amber: A diffuse ache along the inner shin that eases as you warm up, or a stiff Achilles in the morning. Replace the next run with a walk or bike session, keep the calf work, and re-test with 10 single-leg hops in 48 hours.
stopRule.red: Pain at a pinpoint spot on the bone (shin, foot or hip), pain when hopping on one leg, pain at rest or at night, or a limp. Stop running and see a clinician: these are signs of a bone stress injury. Chest pain, unusual breathlessness, palpitations or faintness: stop immediately and get checked.

phaseLearningsPrompts: What was your natural cadence in week 1 vs now, and how did the higher cadence feel at your knees and shins?
Morning-after tissue log: which days did your shins or calves feel anything? Was there a pattern (surface, shoes, back-to-back days)?

phases.title: Aerobic Base: Zone 2 Engine
phases.biomechanicalUnlock: Aerobic adaptations: more mitochondria, denser capillaries, a bigger stroke volume and better fat use at a given pace. Volume rises from about 20 to 35 km/week and the long run reaches 14-16 km.

coreFocus.mechanicalSkill: Run long and easy, holding Zone 2 effort as the distance grows.
coreFocus.mentalModel: Zone 2 is the highest intensity you can hold while lactate stays low (around the first lactate threshold, roughly 60-70% of max heart rate, or a pace where you can speak in full sentences or breathe through the nose). About 80% of your running should live here. It feels too easy; that's the point. Running every run in the moderate 'grey zone' builds fatigue faster than fitness. Formula max-HR estimates are often off by 10+ beats, so trust the talk test over 220-minus-age.

formCues.why: If you can't speak comfortably, slow down, even if it means walking hills.
Hills, heat and wind change pace; keep the effort level.
Tension wastes energy and shortens the stride.

phases.frequency: 3 runs/week: 2 easy Zone 2 runs and 1 long run. Optional 4th easy 20-30 min run or a bike session. Strides 2x/week.

milestones.title: 10 km long run
criteria: Zone 2 throughout.

milestones.title: 30 km week
criteria: No amber flags.

milestones.title: Drift check
criteria: Heart rate drift under 5% on a 60 min run.

milestones.title: Phase 2 Gate: Aerobic Base
criteria: A 14 km (or 90 min) continuous long run in Zone 2, with heart-rate drift under 5% between the first and second halves.
30-35 km weeks for 2 weeks in a row without amber flags.
A faster pace at the same heart rate than in week 7 (log the 5 km split at a fixed HR).

dailyPractice.label: Zone 2 run
dailyPractice.task: Conversational effort the whole way.

dailyPractice.label: Long run
dailyPractice.task: Start at 8 km, add about 1 km/week, cut back every 4th week.

dailyPractice.label: Strides
dailyPractice.task: Relaxed fast on flat ground.

dailyPractice.label: Single-leg strength
dailyPractice.task: Split squats, step-downs and calf raises, slotted into your gym days.

offKeyboardHabit.title: Nasal-breathing lunch walk
offKeyboardHabit.task: 20-30 minutes of brisk walking at lunch with your mouth closed. It counts as easy aerobic volume and undoes some of the sitting.

dos: Heart-rate strap or watch on, and a target zone set.
Water and fuel planned for any run over 60 minutes.
Shin/calf hop test passed.
donts: Don't chase pace. In this phase the pace number is an output, not a target.
Don't increase weekly volume by more than 10% or skip the cutback week.
Don't stack a heavy leg day the day before the long run.

stopRule.amber: Resting heart rate 5-7 bpm above your normal for 2+ days, unusual fatigue, or shin ache. Swap the next run for an easy walk or rest day. A diffuse ache along the inner shin that eases as you warm up, or a stiff Achilles in the morning. Replace the next run with a walk or bike session, keep the calf work, and re-test with 10 single-leg hops in 48 hours.
stopRule.red: Pain at a pinpoint spot on the bone (shin, foot or hip), pain when hopping on one leg, pain at rest or at night, or a limp. Stop running and see a clinician: these are signs of a bone stress injury. Chest pain, unusual breathlessness, palpitations or faintness: stop immediately and get checked.

phaseLearningsPrompts: At the same heart rate, how much faster is your Zone 2 pace than at the start of the phase?
What is your resting heart rate trend? How did sleep and work stress show up in your runs?

phases.title: Threshold & Half-Marathon
phases.biomechanicalUnlock: A higher lactate threshold (LT2) and better running economy. Raising LT2 lets you run faster while staying aerobic; the phase ends with a half marathon.

coreFocus.mechanicalSkill: Hold a 'comfortably hard' threshold effort for 30 minutes, then pace a half marathon evenly.
coreFocus.mentalModel: Lactate threshold is roughly the fastest pace you can hold for about 45-60 minutes before lactate builds faster than you clear it. It feels like RPE 7/10, around 85-90% of max heart rate, a few words at a time. Small doses raise it: keep threshold work to about 10-20% of weekly volume and keep everything else easy.

theoryConcepts: Race pacing: even or negative splits
Polarised weeks: hard days hard, easy days easy

formCues.why: Threshold is controlled. If you are gasping, you are above it.
Your last interval should match your first.
Fatigue shortens cadence and brings back overstriding; count steps when it gets hard.

phases.frequency: 3 runs/week: 1 threshold session, 1 easy, 1 long. 35-42 km/week.

milestones.title: 3 x 10 min threshold
criteria: Even splits.

milestones.title: 30 min tempo
criteria: Continuous, steady heart rate.

milestones.title: 18 km long run
criteria: Last 3 km at half-marathon pace.

milestones.title: Phase 3 Gate: Half Marathon
criteria: Complete a half marathon (race or solo time trial) with an even or negative split: second half within 2% of the first.
30 min continuous tempo at threshold with steady heart rate.

dailyPractice.label: Threshold session
dailyPractice.task: Warm up 15 min. Progress from 3 x 10 min at threshold (2 min jog) to 2 x 20 min, then a 30-40 min continuous tempo. Cool down 10 min.

dailyPractice.label: Easy run
dailyPractice.task: Zone 2 with 6 strides.

dailyPractice.label: Long run
dailyPractice.task: 16-20 km in Zone 2; in the last 4 weeks, the final 3-5 km at half-marathon pace.

dailyPractice.label: Half marathon (week 26)
dailyPractice.task: Taper the final week to about 60% volume. Race at even pace.

offKeyboardHabit.title: Couch stretch + glute bridges
offKeyboardHabit.task: After work: couch stretch 2 x 30 s per side and 10 glute bridges. Hip extension is what lets the stride open up behind you at threshold pace.

dos: Threshold pace and heart rate written down before the session.
Easy day before and after the threshold session.
Gel or fuel tested in training before race day.
donts: Don't turn every run into a tempo.
Don't run threshold sessions faster than prescribed.
Don't try new shoes, gels or breakfast on race day.

stopRule.amber: Morning stiffness in the Achilles or the arch of the foot, or shin ache. Drop the threshold session this week and run easy only. A diffuse ache along the inner shin that eases as you warm up, or a stiff Achilles in the morning. Replace the next run with a walk or bike session, keep the calf work, and re-test with 10 single-leg hops in 48 hours.
stopRule.red: Pain at a pinpoint spot on the bone (shin, foot or hip), pain when hopping on one leg, pain at rest or at night, or a limp. Stop running and see a clinician: these are signs of a bone stress injury. Chest pain, unusual breathlessness, palpitations or faintness: stop immediately and get checked.

phaseLearningsPrompts: What are your threshold pace and heart rate? How do they compare with your gut feel of 'comfortably hard'?
What did you eat and drink in the 24 hours before and during the half marathon? What would you change?

phases.title: Marathon Build: Peak Long Run
phases.biomechanicalUnlock: Glycogen storage, fat use at marathon pace, a trained gut, and tissue durability for 3-4 hours on your feet.

coreFocus.mechanicalSkill: Run a 30-32 km long run with the last 5 km at goal marathon pace, fuelled and without GI trouble.
coreFocus.mentalModel: Your muscles and liver store roughly 400-500 g of glycogen, about 2,000 kcal. If marathon pace relies heavily on carbohydrate, that runs out near 30 km: 'the wall'. Three fixes work together: a bigger aerobic engine that burns more fat at pace, a gut trained to absorb 30-60 g of carbohydrate per hour (up to 90 g with practice), and disciplined pacing.

formCues.why: First gel by 40 min, then every 30-40 min. Don't wait until you feel empty.

formCues.cue: Marathon pace should feel easy for the first 20 km
formCues.why: If it feels like work early, it's too fast.
When form fades, cadence drops first. Count and restore it.

phases.frequency: 3-4 runs/week: long run, a marathon-pace or tempo run, an easy run, and an optional 4th easy run. 40-55 km/week. Drop dragon flags to 2x/week maintenance.

milestones.title: 25 km long run
criteria: Fuelled, Zone 2.

milestones.title: 12 km at marathon pace
criteria: Within a 16 km run.

milestones.title: Phase 4 Gate: Peak Long Run
criteria: A 30-32 km long run (or 3 h, whichever comes first) with the last 5 km at goal marathon pace, fuelled every 30-40 min with no GI distress.
A 45-55 km peak week completed without amber or red flags.

dailyPractice.label: Long run
dailyPractice.task: Build from 20 to 30-32 km (cap about 3 h). Every 3rd long run includes marathon-pace blocks.

dailyPractice.label: Marathon-pace run
dailyPractice.task: 10-16 km with 6-12 km at goal marathon pace.

dailyPractice.label: Easy run
dailyPractice.task: Zone 2.

dailyPractice.label: Gut training
dailyPractice.task: Practise race fuel on every run over 75 minutes.

offKeyboardHabit.title: 8-10k steps
offKeyboardHabit.task: Daily walking volume keeps tissues loaded gently between runs. Keep calf and tibialis raises going 3x/week.

dos: Fuel and fluid packed for runs over 75 minutes.
Legs fresh: no heavy leg day in the 48 hours before the long run.
Hop test passed.
donts: Don't run long runs over 3 hours. The extra time adds damage, not fitness.
Don't skip fuelling to 'train fat burning' on long runs.
Don't increase weekly volume by more than 10% or skip the recovery week every 3rd-4th week.

stopRule.amber: Fatigue that a rest day doesn't fix, elevated resting heart rate, or shin ache. Turn this week into a recovery week. A diffuse ache along the inner shin that eases as you warm up, or a stiff Achilles in the morning. Replace the next run with a walk or bike session, keep the calf work, and re-test with 10 single-leg hops in 48 hours.
stopRule.red: Pain at a pinpoint spot on the bone (shin, foot or hip), pain when hopping on one leg, pain at rest or at night, or a limp. Stop running and see a clinician: these are signs of a bone stress injury. Chest pain, unusual breathlessness, palpitations or faintness: stop immediately and get checked.

phaseLearningsPrompts: What fuelling strategy (product, grams per hour, timing) kept your energy stable from km 25 to 32?
At which km did your form start to fade (cadence drop, shoulders rising)? What cue fixed it?

phases.title: Taper & Race
phases.biomechanicalUnlock: Supercompensation. Fatigue clears faster than fitness decays, so cutting volume while keeping some intensity lets you arrive fresh with fitness intact.

coreFocus.mechanicalSkill: Arrive at the start line rested, then run the marathon to plan.
coreFocus.mentalModel: Nothing you do in the last 10 days makes you fitter, only more tired. Cut volume about 20-30% in taper week 1, 40-50% in week 2, and to about a third in race week, while keeping short marathon-pace segments so the legs remember the rhythm. Phantom aches during a taper are normal.

formCues.cue: Go out at goal pace or slower
formCues.why: The first half should feel controlled. Banking time early costs more later.

formCues.cue: Run the plan, not the crowd
formCues.why: Ignore the people around you for the first 10 km.
Exactly as rehearsed in Phase 4.

phases.frequency: 3 runs/week, shrinking. Dragon flags paused in race week; handstands light (wall holds) only.

milestones.title: Taper done
criteria: Volume dropped as planned.

milestones.title: Pacing plan
criteria: Written and rehearsed.

milestones.title: Race finished
criteria: Marathon or half completed.

milestones.title: Phase 5 Gate: Race
criteria: Finish the marathon with the planned pacing: first half no faster than goal pace, and the two halves within 3% of each other.
Complete the 2-week post-race recovery before any hard session.

dailyPractice.label: ~75% volume
dailyPractice.task: Long run 20-22 km with 8 km at marathon pace.

dailyPractice.label: ~55% volume
dailyPractice.task: Long run 14-16 km, one short MP session.

dailyPractice.label: ~35% volume
dailyPractice.task: 3 short runs with 2-3 km at marathon pace. Carb-load 36-48 h before.

dailyPractice.label: Post-race
dailyPractice.task: 1 week walking or cycling only; no hard running for 2 weeks.

offKeyboardHabit.title: Sleep banking
offKeyboardHabit.task: Aim for 8+ hours in the 2 weeks before the race. The night before the race often sleeps badly; the two nights before that matter more.

dos: Race kit, shoes and fuel all tested in training.
Pacing plan written: target splits for each 5 km.
Carb-load and race-morning breakfast planned.
donts: Don't squeeze in a 'confidence' long run during the taper.
Don't go out faster than goal pace in the first half.
Don't try anything new on race day.

stopRule.amber: Phantom niggles that move around are normal in a taper. Anything that stays in one spot and worsens with walking needs rest, not a test run.
stopRule.red: Pain at a pinpoint spot on the bone (shin, foot or hip), pain when hopping on one leg, pain at rest or at night, or a limp. Stop running and see a clinician: these are signs of a bone stress injury. Chest pain, unusual breathlessness, palpitations or faintness: stop immediately and get checked.

phaseLearningsPrompts: Plan vs reality: where did your pacing deviate and why?
Rate each tissue (shins, calves, knees, hips) the day after and 3 days after the race.

weeklySchedule.assumptions: Morning gym session Mon-Fri. Skill and run sessions go in the evening or at lunch. Put your heaviest leg day on Monday or Wednesday, never the day before the long run.

days.run: Rest (optional easy 4th run in Run Phase 4)

rules: Hard days hard, easy days easy: dragon flag and the quality run share Monday/Thursday so the days between stay genuinely easy.
At least 48 hours between dragon flag sessions (72 hours in DF Phase 4 negatives).
No handstand press work on dragon flag days; both are heavy compression.
If wrists are amber after a heavy pressing day, do 10 minutes of chest-to-wall line work only.
No heavy squats or deadlifts in the 48 hours before the long run.
When running reaches Phase 4 (marathon build), hold dragon flags at 2x/week maintenance and cut gym leg volume by about a third.
Every 4th week is a deload across all three: about 60% of normal volume.

restDayBuff.name: Recovery Buff
restDayBuff.rule: Sunday is a scheduled rest day. Logging it completes the week's streak; skipping it breaks the streak.
checklist: 10 min mobility: wrist CARs, couch stretch, thoracic opener
Log tissue status for wrists, lower back and shins

safety: General guidance for a healthy adult, not medical advice. Get clearance first if you have heart, blood-pressure or eye-pressure conditions, or a history of back, wrist or bone-stress injury.
